title: What Does It Mean to Be Your Authentic Self?
metaTitle: What Does It Mean to Be Your Authentic Self?
metaDescription: Authenticity is better understood as living by your values with self-awareness than as obeying every impulse. Here's what the research actually suggests.
keyFinding: Research suggests authenticity is less about expressing a fixed inner essence than about self-awareness, honesty, and acting in line with your values — and that what feels 'authentic' is shaped partly by what we judge to be good rather than by a true self we simply uncover.
honestAnswer: It probably does not mean what the popular phrase 'express your true self' implies. The research suggests authenticity is better understood as living with self-awareness and honesty, and acting in line with your values — not as obeying whatever you happen to feel in the moment. Being authentic and 'doing what I feel like' are not the same thing.

There is a deeper twist the science points to: what feels authentic is shaped partly by what we judge to be good. People tend to feel most authentic when acting in agreeable, socially desirable ways, and the 'true self' is widely intuited as morally good. That suggests authenticity is partly a values-and-morality judgement rather than a fixed essence waiting to be uncovered — which makes 'be yourself' more of a direction to live by your values than a hidden answer to dig up.
whatDataShows: One influential account, from Michael Kernis and Brian Goldman, breaks authenticity into components rather than treating it as a single feeling: awareness of yourself, unbiased processing of information about yourself, behaviour consistent with your values, and honesty in close relationships. On this view, authenticity is something you practise — self-knowledge plus acting in line with it — not an inner essence you simply reveal.

The picture gets more interesting in research by Katherine Jongman-Sereno and Mark Leary, which finds that people tend to feel most authentic when they are behaving in socially desirable, agreeable ways — and less authentic when acting in less flattering ways, even when that behaviour genuinely reflects them. In other words, the feeling of authenticity tracks how good the behaviour looks more than how truly it represents the person, which complicates the idea that authenticity is just 'expressing the real me.'

Work by Nina Strohminger and Shaun Nichols points the same direction: people across contexts tend to intuit the 'true self' as morally good — when someone changes for the better, we say they have become more themselves; when they change for the worse, we say they have lost themselves. Taken together, these findings suggest that 'authenticity' is partly a moral and values-laden judgement, not a neutral fixed core we uncover.
whyItFeelsDifferent: The common story is intuitive and appealing: that somewhere inside is a fixed, true self, and the task is to find it and express it. That framing feels right because the moments we call authentic are vivid and emotionally clear — but the research suggests those feelings are tracking our values and our sense of being good, not a hidden essence being unveiled.

It also feels different because we rarely notice that we feel most ourselves when we are at our best. The agreeable, generous version of you feels like the 'real' you, while a petty or selfish moment feels 'not like me' — even when both are genuinely you. The feeling of authenticity quietly filters for the flattering, which makes the true-self idea seem more obvious than the evidence supports.

And the cultural messaging leans hard on 'follow your feelings' and 'be true to yourself,' which collapses authenticity into impulse. Because acting on a strong feeling can feel intensely authentic in the moment, it is easy to mistake doing what you feel for living by your values — even when the two pull in opposite directions.
whatResearchSaysToDo: The more supported approach is to treat authenticity as living by your values with self-awareness rather than as obeying every impulse. Kernis and Goldman's components — knowing yourself, processing information about yourself honestly, acting in line with your values, and being honest in close relationships — describe something you can actually practise, rather than a fixed core to locate.

Get clear on what your values actually are, since the research suggests authenticity is bound up with them. When 'be yourself' is vague, identifying the values you want to act on turns it into a usable direction — and helps distinguish acting authentically from simply acting on the strongest feeling available.

Notice when a strong feeling and your values point different ways. Because acting on impulse can feel deeply authentic, the useful skill is separating 'this feels like me right now' from 'this is consistent with who I want to be' — the second is closer to what the research describes as authenticity than the first.
whatDoesNotHelp: Equating authenticity with 'doing whatever I feel' is the most common misstep. The research frames authenticity as self-awareness and value-consistent action, not impulse-following — and acting on a strong feeling can feel authentic in the moment while pulling against the values that more genuinely define you.

Searching for a single fixed 'true self' to uncover is probably chasing something the evidence does not support. Findings that we feel most authentic when behaving agreeably, and that we intuit the true self as morally good, suggest authenticity is partly a values judgement rather than a hidden essence — so the hunt for a fixed core can mislead more than it clarifies.

Using 'I'm just being authentic' to justify unkind behaviour runs against the research too. Since the feeling of authenticity tracks socially desirable, agreeable behaviour and a sense of being good, behaviour that is genuinely harmful is unlikely to be the 'real you' in the sense the science describes — it is closer to acting against your values than expressing them.
realNumbersInContext: This is a conceptual question rather than a numerical one, and the honest answer is a set of converging findings rather than a statistic. Kernis and Goldman frame authenticity as components you practise — awareness, unbiased self-processing, value-consistent behaviour, and relational honesty — rather than a fixed essence.

Two findings reshape the popular picture: Jongman-Sereno and Leary report that people tend to feel most authentic when acting in socially desirable, agreeable ways, and Strohminger and Nichols find that the 'true self' is widely intuited as morally good. Together these suggest authenticity is partly a moral and values-laden judgement, not a neutral core we uncover — which is why 'live by your values with self-awareness' is a more defensible reading than 'obey every impulse.' These are research patterns; treat any single precise figure in this area with caution.

faqs.question: Does being authentic mean doing whatever I feel?
faqs.answer: The research suggests not. Authenticity is better understood as self-awareness and acting in line with your values, not following every impulse. Acting on a strong feeling can feel intensely authentic in the moment while pulling against the values that more genuinely define who you want to be.

faqs.question: Is there a fixed 'true self' I need to find?
faqs.answer: Probably not in the way the popular phrase implies. Findings that we feel most authentic when behaving agreeably (Jongman-Sereno and Leary) and that we intuit the true self as morally good (Strohminger and Nichols) suggest authenticity is partly a values judgement, not a fixed essence waiting to be uncovered.

faqs.question: Why do I feel most 'like myself' when I'm at my best?
faqs.answer: Research suggests the feeling of authenticity tracks how good and socially desirable our behaviour is more than how truly it represents us. The agreeable, generous version of you tends to feel like the 'real' you, while a petty moment feels 'not like me' — even when both are genuinely you.

faqs.question: What does authenticity actually consist of?
faqs.answer: One influential account (Kernis and Goldman) describes it as components you can practise: awareness of yourself, processing information about yourself honestly, behaving consistently with your values, and honesty in close relationships. On this view authenticity is something you do, not an essence you simply reveal.

faqs.question: Can 'being authentic' justify treating people badly?
faqs.answer: The research points the other way. Because the feeling of authenticity tracks agreeable, value-consistent behaviour and a sense of being good, genuinely harmful behaviour is unlikely to be the 'real you' in the sense the science describes — it's closer to acting against your values than expressing them.

dataSources: Kernis, M. H., & Goldman, B. M. — research on the components of authenticity (awareness, unbiased processing, behaviour, relational orientation).
Jongman-Sereno, K. P., & Leary, M. R. — research on feeling authentic and the role of socially desirable behaviour.
Strohminger, N., & Nichols, S. — research on the true self as intuited to be morally good.
